title: Institutional Controls for Tokenized Asset Rights and Custody
subtitle: Eligibility, segregation of duties, network permissioning, recovery and operational resilience
abstract: Tokenization may provide cryptographic integrity for a specified state transition while failing to establish that the transition was permitted, legal, complete or recoverable. Institutional controls include actor identity, legal authority, investor eligibility, custody access, transaction limits, governance of upgrade keys, privacy, segregation and business-continuity procedures. This report distinguishes permissioned participation from confidentiality and defines a control model for the TSP-01 workstreams.

evidence.heading: The nature of risks does not disappear on a ledger
evidence.body: The Financial Stability Board's 2024 tokenisation assessment highlights vulnerabilities involving liquidity, leverage, interconnectedness, operational resilience and structural complexity. The BIS/CPMI work notes that new digital infrastructures require appropriate governance, credit and liquidity controls as well as legal safeguards. A valid token balance is a record of a digital state, not evidence of a valid custodian segregation arrangement or regulator-approved transfer.

evidence.heading: Tokenized securities remain securities with governing rights
evidence.body: The SEC's nonbinding staff statement and Trading and Markets FAQ address how security ownership, intermediaries, recordkeeping and custody may interact with DLT. These sources do not grant general permission to issue tokenized securities or dispense with transfer-agent and investor protection responsibilities. Controlled instruments must define their legal rights and operational agents before smart-contract role assignment.

evidence.heading: Security controls are broader than a token interface
evidence.body: ERC-7518 and other token interface proposals can specify authorization and compliance mechanisms, but contract standards alone cannot establish off-chain identity, adequacy of legal documentation, sanctions status, fiduciary duties or independent audit. A permissioned public EVM application can require eligible wallets while its transaction events remain publicly observable. Confidentiality requires a separate privacy architecture and selective data-disclosure policy.

architecture.heading: Actor and mandate model
architecture.body: Define issuer, registrar, custodian, payment agent, investor, broker, trading venue, settlement coordinator and auditor as different legal and operational principals. Assign each explicit authority: issuance approval, custody attestation, eligible transfer, payout instruction, manual override, pause and forensic access. No single routine operator should be able to create outstanding financial claims, release their backing and suppress the independent audit in one transaction path.

architecture.heading: Permissioning, privacy and public liquidity
architecture.body: A public chain with permissioned contract access may enable transparent settlement-event evidence and public price discovery while blocking transfers to ineligible persons. Public liquidity is not assured by chain availability; eligible counterparty depth, broker integration, legal transferability and trading venue rules determine executable markets. Wallet allowlists also do not provide confidential economic detail by themselves. Keep sensitive identities off-chain or use legally appropriate disclosure technology.

architecture.heading: Upgrade and emergency power
architecture.body: Each mint, forced transfer, freeze, upgrade, key rotation or emergency pause needs an authorized policy version, quorum, reason, effective timestamp and independent audit artifact. A freeze can protect investors from a compromised key but can also deny property use or create governance concentration. Specify appeal, notification and recovery paths, including what may happen if the issuer, operator or custodian becomes insolvent.

architecture.heading: Operational resilience and loss containment
architecture.body: Test custodian outage, validator failure, lost private keys, delayed bank settlement, duplicate transaction signals, issuer bankruptcy and compliance rule changes. A valid business-continuity plan does not require pretending the ledger can reverse all external transactions. It defines pending rights, safe no-mint states, evidence preservation and an institution responsible for compensation or court-directed correction.

case.title: Synthetic authority matrix for a restricted receipt system
case.setup: A receipt issuer maintains 50,000 eligible units backed by externally verified assets. Five actors operate different workflows, and the auditor cannot create or seize investor claims.
rows: Authorize eligible issuance within approved program
Update beneficial owner and token eligibility
Cannot change custody proof by itself
Accept valid payment and delivery instructions
Read and challenge authority; no ordinary mint rights
case.formula: Authorization rule = ValidIdentity ∧ AuthorizedRole ∧ MandateVersion ∧ TransactionLimits ∧ ValidUnderlyingRight. A valid signature is necessary but insufficient if the mandated action is prohibited.
case.interpretation: Segregated authority makes a malicious or mistaken single actor less able to fabricate rights or hide obligations. The degree of independence must be evaluated against real organizational ownership.

risks: An upgrade key can mint rights without custody confirmation.
Timelocks or controlled emergency governance and independent verification.
Wallet allowlist reveals transaction sizes and counterparties on public EVM.
Selective disclosure, address management and confidentiality design.
Holder loses a key while legal rights persist.
Authorized identity recovery without uncontrolled seizure.
tests: Attempt unauthorized mint, blacklisted transfer and privileged upgrade using adversarial roles; verify prevention and audit evidence.
Run a custodian outage while investors trade on a venue and define safe issuance, transfer and redemption states.
Compare permissioned public EVM, private consortium ledger and centralized registry against confidentiality, auditability and liquidity-access requirements.
conclusion: The security boundary for institutional tokenization is the combination of enforceable rights, independent assets, governance authority, privacy and failure recovery. A permissioned token is only one component of that assurance architecture.

title: Independent Financial-State Verification: Completeness, Valuation and Reconciliation
subtitle: Proof that the known token ledger is not missing obligations, backing assets or unsettled positions
abstract: Blockchains can make transactions tamper-evident while leaving the population of underlying claims invisible. Financial assurance must independently establish completeness of obligations, legitimacy of custodial backing, valuation and contractual discharge. This report develops a three-record audit model—rights registry, token ledger and monetary/custody evidence—with controls for mismatches that a purely on-chain balance check would overlook.

evidence.heading: Auditability is not the same as data visibility
evidence.body: The FSB and IMF analyses of tokenized finance identify operational risk, governance concentration and interconnectedness as material considerations. A visible transfer history does not identify unrecorded obligations or whether an off-chain security still exists. The auditor therefore needs a population-level assertion from an independent legal register, contract list, custodian or bank, not only the digital token issuer's own statements.

evidence.heading: Asset servicing produces off-chain evidence
evidence.body: Project Guardian's fund and collateral lifecycle frameworks include transfer agents, custody, asset administration and other operators that must account for legal and economic changes outside a token contract. A corporate action can change entitlements without changing wallet balances on the announcement date. Similarly, receipt burns do not necessarily prove asset delivery or final cash payments. An external evidence pipeline is a research requirement, not proof of existing market practice.

evidence.heading: Source authority and ledger semantics affect verification
evidence.body: The BIS Project Meridian illustrates coordinated asset transfer and money settlement among independently operated systems, while Project Agorá studies a shared platform with institutional roles. Neither structure eliminates the question of whether an authorized source reported all claims. Reconciliation should also identify statuses such as pending, rejected, final and legally disputed rather than treating every interface event as settled.

architecture.heading: Three distinct audit assertions
architecture.body: Existence: tokenized rights reported by the issuer correspond to valid underlying assets or claims. Completeness: all relevant legally outstanding claims are included, even if not already known to the token system. Rights and obligations: the amount, holder, currency, restrictions and seniority match valid documentation. A fourth financial assertion concerns settlement: discharged positions have final money or asset evidence and balancing accounts.

architecture.heading: Cross-system reconciliation equations
architecture.body: For a depositary receipt, eligible backing capacity minus token claims should be non-negative under the contract's conversion ratio. For a payment obligation, approved outstanding should equal approved opening balance plus valid increases minus final settlements and recognized cancellations. A token contract can supply one side of each equation, but another independent register must provide the economic side. Exceptions must be classified by timing, quantity, ownership or legal status.

architecture.heading: Event provenance and policy versions
architecture.body: Link each asset, token and monetary event to a unique economic-event ID and issuer/custodian/bank source. Preserve signed custody statements, bank confirmation IDs, legal instrument identifiers, authorized corporate action evidence, hash references, policy versions and correction history. Data quality rules should detect stale custody files, duplicate transfers, timestamp mismatches, missing holder records and unapproved manual adjustments.

architecture.heading: Assurance under privacy constraints
architecture.body: An independent reviewer may need proof of balance completeness without seeing every investor's confidential details. Provide encrypted or restricted evidence layers, aggregate reconciliation, authorized attestations and selective review of underlying contracts. A published Merkle root of the token list does not prove the issuer's liabilities are complete if undisclosed obligations were never placed in the source list.

case.title: Synthetic custody discrepancy audit
case.setup: A custodian report shows 1,200 underlying shares, each supporting 10 receipts. The issuer reports 11,000 outstanding receipts. Of the custodied shares, 150 are independently identified as pledged to another secured obligation and cannot back freely redeemable receipts under the assumed contract.
rows: No new issue; investigate collateral and holder rights
case.formula: Eligible shares = 1,200 − 150 = 1,050. Eligible receipt capacity = 1,050 × 10 = 10,500. Outstanding receipts 11,000 ⇒ 500 receipt units of undercoverage.
case.interpretation: A simplistic on-chain supply check could report 11,000 valid token units. The economically decisive discrepancy only appears after external custody and encumbrance evidence.

risks: An issuer excludes private bilateral claims from its reported token liability population.
Independent contracts, investor statements and servicing records included in audit.
A once-valid backing report is reused after securities leave the account.
Fresh timestamp requirements and independent custodian reconciliation.
Operator selects both asset population and final audit conclusion.
Separate institutional access, documented challenge and reproducible evidence.
tests: Reconstruct outstanding rights from external asset and obligations registers, intentionally inserting a missing investor and an ineligible pledged unit.
Verify journal-to-bank settlement for both fully and partially redeemed claims, with replay attempts and corrective entries.
Demonstrate rights verification under masked investor identifiers while preserving legally authorized audit disclosure.
conclusion: Independent financial assurance is a claim-completeness and rights problem, not a token explorer feature. TRR, TSR, SPE and AFG should share evidence protocols that enable an independent reviewer to detect omitted assets, overissued receipts, disputed claims and unrecognized settlements.
